To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the chewing process in terms swallowing threshold parameters is not as effective in complete denture and overdenture wearers as in subjects with complete natural teeth.
subjects with overdentures had significantly more chewing cycles until swallowing and significantly larger particle sizes after swallowing compared to subjects with natural dentitions.
subjects with complete denture (with or without overdenture) need significantly more cycles and time until ‘swalling’ compared to subjects without denture.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the chewing process of subjects wearing complete dentures and over-dentures and with the comparison of these results with data obtained from complete natural dentitions as reference.
the swallowing threshold parameters of the chewing process in subjects with complete denture and overdentures and the comparison with the reference group of subjects with complete natural den-tition.
the chewing process of subjects with different types of complete dentures (complete dentures and overdenteures) and the influence of the denture type on swallowing threshold parameters.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
subjects with overdentures and complete dentures have significantly more difficulties to ‘swallow’ a test food than subjects with complete natural den-titions.
the chewing and swallowing process is significantly affected by the presence of dentures.
the swallowing process in subjects with complete denture (including overdenture) was slower and more energy-consuming compared to subjects with a natural dentition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the chewing process and the ‘swallowing threshold’ parameters are significantly influenced by the type of the prosthetic restoration.
the chewing efficiency of subjects with complete natural and complete denture prostheses is not significantly different.
chewing is a highly individual process and is influenced by the number of remaining teeth, the denture type, the mandibular height, the chewing time and the type of food particles used for the test.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the chewing efficiency of subjects with complete natural and complete denture prosthesis is different, and that subjects with complete denture pro-thesis need more chewing cycles until ‘swallo-wing’ than subjects with complete natural pro-thesis.
chewing efficiency and swallowing threshold parameters in subjects with complete denture (including overdenture) were significantly lower compared to subjects with a complete natural dentition.
the chewing process in subjects with complete denture (including overdenture) groups is significantly different from subjects with natural dentition groups.
